worker_target_description: Study 1 separate-evaluations perceived generosity comparison of $45 scarf versus $55 coat; randomized mutually exclusive scarf and coat groups, excluding the joint-evaluation extension.
worker_notes: Identity inspected independently: publisher HTML excerpt bears the exact replication title, DOI 10.1525/collabra.77859, Collabra: Psychology (2023) 9 (1): 77859, and matching visible author names Anna Thao Bich Nguyen, Bo Ley Cheng, and Gilad Feldman. It contains primary report methods/results, not a preregistration or secondary account. The cached parse is partial (visible author list incomplete and excerpt ends during Study 2); no inference of full-work absence is made. Target identified by gift amounts, perceived-generosity measure, and explicitly labeled Study 1 separate-evaluations results, not input order or numerical matching. Analytic N derivation: 135 coat + 131 scarf = 266 participants, from explicitly randomized mutually exclusive final groups after three overall refusal exclusions. The joint extension is outside this test; its inconsistent printed counts (134 overall versus 133 in the Study 1 vignette description) do not enter the sum. N is not inferred from Welch degrees of freedom. Only n_r assigned; all other fields are placeholders and must not overwrite existing verified values.

coding_context.description: Participants receiving the $45 scarf will consider their friend more generous than those receiving the $55 coat.
coding_context.reported_success_quote:
We found support for “less is better” across all studies (N = 403; Study 1 original d = 0.70
[0.24,1.15], replication d = 0.99 [0.72,1.26]; Study 2 original d = 0.74 [0.12,1.35],
replication d = 0.32 [0.07,0.56]; Study 4 original d = 0.97 [0.43,1.50], replication d = 0.76
[0.50,1.02]), with weaker support for “more is better”.
